title: Ginject Performance Characteristics
purpose: Document performance bottlenecks and optimization opportunities

components.cost: trie lookup bounded by the route tree size; static routes through a map

dependency_resolution_cost.source: docs/design/0006-injection.md; core/README.md holds the benchmark table
dependency_resolution_cost.model: one argument plan per handler built at Create(); a call is one reflect.Value.Call plus the accessors and pipes
dependency_resolution_cost.optimization: no per-request type walking, key building, map lookups or argument-list construction; pipe prototypes built once

routing_performance.source: docs/design/0002-routing.md; routing/README.md and internal/ds/README.md hold the benchmark tables

static_route.mechanism: map of fully static routes per (method, version), probed before the trie

parameter_route.mechanism: trie walk by index, one map lookup per static segment, values collected into one slice at the match
parameter_route.time: about 170-200 ns, 1 alloc of 16 B per value slice (no caller buffer: heavy technique H1 not approved)

miss.mechanism: same walk, nothing allocated; a 404 calls Match twice (version, then NEUTRAL)

routing_performance.limits: paths over 4,096 bytes or 64 segments never match (404)
routing_performance.no_regex: route matching uses no regexp; globs are matched by a linear scan per '*'

dependency_resolution.mitigation: use fewer parameters, cache handler signatures (already done)

exception_handling.issue: panic recovery + stack trace capture expensive
exception_handling.mitigation: avoid exceptions in hot path, use bool returns

middleware_chain.mitigation: keep middleware count low (2-3 global max)

request_context.issue: ctx creates the context, binds the request and writes the response on every request
request_context.cost: measured (ctx benchmarks, i7-9750H): Init + Reset 113 ns / 1 alloc; Text 55 ns; JSON of a small Map 880 ns; warm Body.Bind of 5 fields with a nested struct 962 ns (BindValue 382 ns); Query.Bind of 2 fields 311 ns (BindValue 162 ns)
request_context.mitigation: binding plan per struct type (ctx.BinderOf, cached); BindValue when the FieldLevels are not needed; see ctx/README.md Performance notes

json_marshaling.mitigation: use binary format for high-throughput APIs

websocket_fanout.mitigation: use topic patterns to reduce subscribers

opportunity_1.name: Typed handler call without reflect.Value.Call
opportunity_1.current: done for the argument list (stack array, design 0006); the call itself stays reflect.Value.Call (Q1 of design 0006: unsafe or an opt-in method-value API, neither approved)
opportunity_1.potential_savings: about 200 ns per request for the signatures it could cover

opportunity_3.name: Reduce guard/interceptor reflection
opportunity_3.current: done (design 0005): guards, interceptors and filters are called through compiled method values, interceptor state is a per-request list on the context
opportunity_3.potential_savings: realized: about 350 ns and 1 allocation per layer call

opportunity_5.name: Connection pooling for WS send channels

throughput.broker_publishes_per_second: not benchmarked end-to-end; memorybroker.Publish itself measured in isolation at ~18-24 microseconds/op fanning out to 1000 exact-topic subscribers, ~2 microseconds/op for 10 mixed exact+prefix+global subscribers (see memorybroker/broker_bench_test.go) — do not cite a messages/sec figure without re-measuring, this field previously stated an unverified 100K-1M

http_server_fixed_limits.note: core.App has no per-handler timeout and no configurable body cap — all fixed at New()/Listen() time, no public setters
http_server_fixed_limits.max_request_body_bytes: DefaultMaxRequestBodyBytes = 10MB, enforced via http.MaxBytesReader in ServeHTTP; exceeding it panics a 413 from ctx.Body(), not a raw error
http_server_fixed_limits.caveat: these bound the connection, not handler execution time — a slow handler is not interrupted by any of them

optimization_checklist: [ ] Profile actual hot paths before optimizing
[ ] Use topic patterns to reduce WS fanout
[ ] Avoid exceptions in normal flow (use bool returns)
[ ] Keep global middleware count low (2-3 max)
[ ] Use binary serialization for high-throughput APIs
[ ] Batch database operations instead of per-request queries
